lessons.title: Straight-line graphs and gradient
lessons.programRef: O Level Mathematics — Functions and graphs (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Find the gradient of a line from two points and read it from y = mx + c.
Find the equation of a line, parallel and perpendicular lines.
Find the midpoint and the length of a line segment.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Gradient and equation
blocks.md: For two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ the gradient is the rise over the run. A line with gradient m and y-intercept c has equation y = mx + c:

blocks.title: Parallel and perpendicular
blocks.md: Parallel lines have the **same gradient**. Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1: if one has gradient m, the other has $-\frac{1}{m}$. A horizontal line has gradient 0; a vertical line has no gradient.

blocks.title: Midpoint and distance
blocks.md: Midpoint M and length AB of the segment joining $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$:
blocks.tex: M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right) \qquad AB = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Subtracting coordinates in different orders: $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_1 - x_2}$ gives the wrong sign.
- Using gradient 'rise = horizontal': always vertical change over horizontal change.
- A negative reciprocal means both flipping **and** changing the sign.

blocks.title: Example 1: equation of a line
blocks.statement: Find the equation of the line through A(1, 2) and B(4, 11).

steps.md: Use y = 3x + c with A(1, 2): 2 = 3 + c, so c = −1.

blocks.title: Example 2: parallel, perpendicular, midpoint
blocks.statement: (a) Line parallel to y = 2x + 5 through (3, 1). (b) Midpoint and length of the segment from P(2, −1) to Q(8, 5).
steps: (a) Gradient 2: y = 2x + c; 1 = 6 + c, so c = −5: y = 2x − 5.

lessons.title: Quadratic graphs and graphical solutions
lessons.programRef: O Level Mathematics — Functions and graphs (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Draw the graph of a quadratic function from a table of values.
Read roots, the turning point and the line of symmetry.
Solve equations graphically by drawing a second graph.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The parabola
blocks.md: The graph of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ is a smooth U-shaped curve (**parabola**). If a > 0 it opens upwards with a minimum; if a < 0 it opens downwards with a maximum. It is symmetrical about a vertical line through its **turning point**, at $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$.

blocks.title: Method: using the graph
blocks.md:
1. Make a table of values and plot the points; join with a **smooth curve**.
2. The **roots** of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are where the curve meets the x-axis.
3. To solve $f(x) = k$, draw the line y = k and read the x-values where it cuts the curve.
4. To solve $f(x) = mx + n$, draw that line too.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Joining points with straight segments: the curve must be smooth, flat at the turning point.
- Reading only one root: there are usually two (symmetrical about the turning point).
- Choosing a scale that is too small: use the whole sheet.

blocks.title: Example 1: table and roots
blocks.statement: Complete the table for $y = x^2 - 2x - 3$ for x from −2 to 4 and find the roots, the minimum point and the solutions of $x^2 - 2x - 3 = 2$.
steps: Roots: the curve meets the x-axis at x = −1 and x = 3. Minimum point (1, −4).
Line y = 2 cuts the curve where $x = 1 \pm \sqrt{6}$, i.e. x ≈ −1.45 and x ≈ 3.45.

blocks.title: Example 2: a second graph
blocks.statement: Using the same curve, which line should be drawn to solve $x^2 - 3x - 2 = 0$? Give the solutions to 1 d.p.
steps: Start from $x^2 - 3x - 2 = 0$ and write it as $x^2 - 2x - 3 = x - 1$ (add x and subtract 1 on both sides). So draw y = x − 1.
The line cuts the curve at x ≈ −0.6 and x ≈ 3.6 (exactly $\frac{3 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}$).

lessons.title: Distance-time and speed-time graphs
lessons.programRef: O Level Mathematics — Functions and graphs (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Interpret speed-time graphs: gradient = acceleration, area = distance.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Two kinds of graph
blocks.md: **Distance-time**: gradient = speed; a horizontal line means stopped. **Speed-time**: gradient = acceleration (negative = deceleration); a horizontal line means constant speed; **area under the graph = distance travelled**.

blocks.title: Formulae
blocks.md: Speed, distance and time, and average speed:

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Confusing the two graphs: on a speed-time graph a horizontal line is **not** stopped (it is steady speed).
- Mixing units: km/h with minutes, m/s with km.
- Average speed is not the average of two speeds unless times are equal.

blocks.title: Example 1: speed-time graph
blocks.statement: A vehicle accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s, travels at 20 m/s for 30 s, then slows to rest in 20 s. Find the acceleration, the total distance and the average speed.
steps: Distance = area of the trapezium = ½ × (30 + 60) × 20 = 900 m.

blocks.title: Example 2: distance-time graph
blocks.statement: A cyclist rides 24 km in 1.5 hours, rests for 0.5 hour, then rides back 24 km in 2 hours. Find the speed on each stage and the average speed for the whole trip.
steps: Out: 24 ÷ 1.5 = 16 km/h. Rest: 0 km/h. Back: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 km/h.
Total distance 48 km; total time 1.5 + 0.5 + 2 = 4 hours.

lessons.title: Inequalities on a graph and linear programming
lessons.programRef: O Level Mathematics — Functions and graphs (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Draw a straight line from an inequality and shade the region.
Find the maximum or minimum of a quantity at a vertex of the region.
reviewNotes: Linear programming may be at the edge of the O Level syllabus: check.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Method: shading a region
blocks.md:
1. Draw the boundary line: **solid** for ≤ or ≥, **dashed** for < or >.
2. Pick a test point (the origin if it is not on the line) and test the inequality.
3. If true, shade (or keep) the side containing the point; otherwise the other side.
4. The region that satisfies **all** inequalities is where the shadings overlap.

blocks.title: Linear programming
blocks.md: To maximise or minimise a quantity such as P = 3x + 2y over a region bounded by lines, evaluate it at the **vertices** (corners) of the region: the largest and smallest values occur there.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Drawing a solid line for a strict inequality.
- Choosing a test point that lies on the line.
- Forgetting that x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 are often implied by the context (numbers of items).

blocks.title: Example 1: describing a region
blocks.statement: The triangle with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 3) is shaded. Give three inequalities that describe it.
steps: The sides on the axes give x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.
The slanted side passes through (4, 0) and (0, 3): 3x + 4y = 12.
The origin gives 0 ≤ 12, so the region is 3x + 4y ≤ 12.

blocks.title: Example 2: linear programming
blocks.statement: A trader makes profit P = 3x + 2y (in thousands of FCFA) selling x boxes of cocoa and y boxes of coffee with x + y ≤ 6, x ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Find the maximum profit.
steps: The vertices of the region are (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 2) and (0, 6).

lessons.title: Functions and mappings
lessons.programRef: O Level Mathematics — Functions and graphs (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use function notation f(x) and evaluate functions.
State the domain and range of a simple function.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Function
blocks.md: A **function** assigns to every input x of the **domain** exactly one output f(x); the set of outputs is the **range**. We write f(x) = 3x − 2 or f: x → 3x − 2. A function maps each input to one output only.

blocks.title: Composite and inverse
blocks.md:
- **fg(x)** means 'do g first, then f': fg(x) = f(g(x)). The order matters.
- **Inverse** f⁻¹ undoes f: write y = f(x), make x the subject, then swap the names. Check that f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.
- The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Reading fg as 'f first': g is applied first.
- Confusing $f^{-1}(x)$ with $\frac{1}{f(x)}$.
- Forgetting that some inputs may be excluded: $\frac{1}{x}$ is not defined at x = 0.

blocks.title: Example 1: evaluate and invert
blocks.statement: f(x) = 3x − 2. Find f(5), the value of x when f(x) = 10, and the inverse function.
steps: Let y = 3x − 2, so x = (y + 2)/3. Hence f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3; check f⁻¹(10) = 4.

blocks.title: Example 2: composite functions
blocks.statement: f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = x². Find gf(−1), fg(3), and solve fg(x) = gf(x).
